video_title: MacroVoices #558 Mike Alkin: Uranium at a Crossroads
gist: Mike Alkin (Sachem Cove) argues the uranium bull case rests solely on a structural deficit for the existing reactor fleet and is unrelated to AI, yet uranium equities are being sold as part of AI baskets just as fuel buyers turn bullish, reported contract prices (~$98-99/lb) understate realized triple-digit pricing, and costs and fuel-cycle services have surged. He frames physical uranium vs. miners as a risk-tolerance choice and sees asymmetric upside from restocking, a broken cost curve, and possible new-build announcements; the market desk adds a SPUT discount bull call spread and a hawkish-Fed macro backdrop.

themes.theme: Uranium thesis decoupled from AI, but traded as AI

insights.claim: Mike Alkin's core uranium thesis is that there is not enough economically viable uranium to supply the existing fleet of about 440 operating reactors (just over 420 producing power) plus a pipeline of roughly 80 new reactors.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: The bull case rests on existing-fleet demand, so it should survive an AI capex bust even if prices of equities do not.
insights.quote: There is not enough economically viable uranium to satisfy the world's existing reactor fleet of 440 operating reactors

insights.claim: According to Alkin, nuclear power has shifted from roughly a 0.5% annual grower when his uranium trade began to a 4-5% annual grower, independent of data center demand.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Structural demand growth acceleration is the under-appreciated driver, not AI headlines.
insights.quote: it was a nuclear was maybe a half percent grower and now it's a four to 5% grower

insights.claim: Alkin argues that even if no data center ever opened, the uranium market would still face a massive structural deficit, so AI is irrelevant to the fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Treat AI-driven selloffs in uranium names as sentiment dislocations rather than thesis changes.
insights.quote: If a data center didn't open, there is still a massive structural deficit in uranium.

insights.claim: Bank-created baskets (Goldman, Morgan and others) lump nuclear and uranium names into AI/data-center and momentum baskets, so uranium equities trade on flows rather than fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Expect uranium miners to move with AI-basket de-risking; size positions for flow-driven drawdowns.
insights.quote: it becomes facts be damned, it becomes flows

insights.claim: Alkin blames uranium junior miners for marketing themselves as part of the AI and data-center trade, which invited the current guilt-by-association selloff when AI capex came into question.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Juniors with heavy AI-narrative marketing may be most exposed to basket selling.

insights.claim: Erik Townsend frames the setup as a sentiment crossover: Wall Street sentiment on uranium equities has collapsed to Liberation Day lows on AI capex bust fears and Democrat political threats, while fuel buyers have turned bullish and spot and term prices are rising.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host)
insights.so_what: Divergence between end-user (buyer) sentiment and equity sentiment is a classic value setup in the miners.

insights.claim: Alkin lists rising interest rates (hurting long-lived assets), uncertain mine build costs, data-center delays and NIMBY opposition, and a Democratic takeover as drivers knocking down uranium equities day-to-day.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Monitor rate moves and political headlines as short-term catalysts for the equities, not the commodity.

insights.claim: Townsend warns that Chuck Schumer has intimated the post-blue-tsunami Democrat platform could make AI and data centers public enemy number one, which could cause a wipeout in nuclear names that are basketed with AI.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host)
insights.so_what: Political risk to AI capex is a real tail risk for uranium equities; consider hedging or convexity.

insights.claim: Kazatomprom's 2018-2019 IPO prospectus forecast costs of about $13-14/lb by 2026, but its actual cost today is about $38.45/lb, and over $55/lb if normalized to the tenge rate assumed in the prospectus.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Even the world's lowest-cost producer needs far higher prices than assumed, implying the whole cost curve is too low.

insights.claim: Kazakhstan supplies 41% of global uranium, with state-owned Kazatomprom accounting for about half of that and joint ventures the rest.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Supply concentration in one Eastern state is a key geopolitical risk for Western utilities.
insights.quote: Kazakhstan is 41% of global uranium supply

insights.claim: Uranium development and production projects have repeatedly missed promises, with costs coming in 80-90% to a couple hundred percent above guidance and production targets falling short by 50-70%.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Single-name mining risk is high; the aggregate shortfall is bullish for price but bearish for individual project holders.
insights.quote: production targets that are down by 50 60 70%

insights.claim: Alkin's framework: investors with low risk tolerance should express the uranium view through the physical commodity to avoid mining risk, while those seeking torque should own equities but favor proven producers who deserve a scarcity premium.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Choose vehicle by risk tolerance; within equities, pay up for demonstrated operators.

insights.claim: Cameco said on its conference call it is getting triple-digit pricing on contracts even though the reported long-term contract price is about $98-99/lb, which Alkin calls the key overlooked takeaway from its weak quarter.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Realized contract prices are running above published indicators; the reported price understates the market.
insights.quote: Kamico told you they had tripledigit pricing and that's not being price reported

insights.claim: When Cameco bought its 49% Westinghouse stake in 2022 the contract price was about $49/lb and Cameco traded around 31x EBITDA; with prices more than doubled since, Alkin estimates Cameco now trades at roughly 8-9x EBITDA under reasonable Westinghouse assumptions, which he calls stupid for the West's dominant producer.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Cameco's valuation looks compressed relative to its strategic position and the price environment.

insights.claim: Cameco does not guide quarterly (it gives annual guidance), so a few-week mine delay becomes a headline 'miss' that algorithms sell, which Alkin views as noise.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Headline-driven drops in Cameco on quarterly results can be buying opportunities for long-term holders.

insights.claim: Uranium equities have pulled back significantly in recent months to valuations last seen four or five years ago, even though uranium has gone from $17-18/lb to over $100 and some contract ceilings sit in the $150s.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Equity valuations have de-rated against a much stronger commodity backdrop, creating asymmetry.

insights.claim: Scale is everything in uranium mining: small projects of 0.5-2 million pounds per year are being hammered on costs.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Favor large-scale producers and be skeptical of small developers' cost estimates.

insights.claim: Townsend notes a split among respected uranium investors: some are selling physical (SPUT) to buy Cameco after its earnings miss, while others are selling Cameco to buy SPUT to avoid AI-basket risk.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host)
insights.so_what: Positioning is divided, reflecting the miners-vs-metal debate.

insights.claim: Uranium price reporters peg the price to the lowest offer heard on a contract rather than where contracts actually strike, so reported prices lag real transaction levels.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Published term prices likely understate the true market; watch producer commentary for realized prices.
insights.quote: They price where the lowest offer came in on a contract that they've heard about.

insights.claim: Alkin rejects price reporters' fungibility rationale because about 70% of uranium is produced in the East while about 70% is consumed in the West, where there are massive deficits.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Geographic and geopolitical mismatch argues for a Western price premium.
insights.quote: 70% of it is produced in the east and yet 70% is consumed in the west

insights.claim: Utilities are contracting only a little over half of their annual needs, yet the long-term uranium price has quadrupled, which Alkin says shows how tight the market already is.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Price strength without replacement-rate contracting implies a much bigger move when contracting normalizes.
insights.quote: The long-term price of uranium, long-term price has quadrupled.

insights.claim: Roughly 75-85% of uranium is bought under long-term contracts because utilities need security of supply and cannot fuel-switch, so long-term contracts guide the market.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Track term contracting volumes and term price rather than spot for the real signal.

insights.claim: Fuel buyers have destocked for about 15 years; if consumption is roughly 200-230 million pounds, they will need to buy 250-270 million pounds annually to restock, supply that does not currently exist.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Restocking demand on top of consumption is the catalyst for the next leg higher.
insights.quote: when you destock, what do you need to do? You need to restock.

insights.claim: Utilities need to contract over a couple of billion pounds of uranium by 2040, and there are not enough economically viable pounds above ground to meet it, which Alkin likens to putting a pig through a python.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Large contracting backlog through 2040 underpins multi-year price support.
insights.quote: it is going to be like putting a pig through a python

insights.claim: Requests for proposals from utilities now draw very few bids, versus 7-12 or more a few years ago, because miners do not want to sell their books at current prices.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: A sellers' market in RFPs signals upward pressure on term prices.

insights.claim: Current long-term contract terms include ceilings of about $150-160/lb with floors of $70-75, alongside a spot price around $91-92.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Contract ceilings imply producers and buyers both see substantially higher prices as plausible.

insights.claim: Alkin expects a panic-driven price spike could be triggered by just one small utility with one or two reactors that buys infrequently and is not commercially sophisticated entering the market.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Watch for an unsophisticated utility's RFP as a potential catalyst for a price gap-up.
insights.quote: all it takes is one of them

themes.theme: Cost curve and fuel cycle services

insights.claim: Industry forecasters' weighted-average production cost rose from $24/lb (2019) to $27 (2021), $30 (2023) and $38 (2025), while Kazatomprom alone is at $38.45, so Alkin says the cost curve is broken and needs a full reset.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: An upward-shifting cost curve raises the incentive price floor for uranium.
insights.quote: the cost curve's broken it needs to be entirely reset

insights.claim: Alkin argues pure-play uranium miners must be valued on all-in costs, not cash or all-in sustaining costs, because a company cannot run a mine if it cannot run a company.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Use all-in costs when estimating incentive price; it is far above consensus operating-cost curves.

insights.claim: Conversion prices rose from about $4/kg to over $60 and enrichment from about $30 to $200+, while uranium is up about 4x; Alkin expects the product (uranium) to catch up to the service price moves.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Fuel-cycle services have already squeezed; uranium is the laggard with catch-up potential.
insights.quote: the product always catches or the product will catch up to where the service move has been

insights.claim: The conversion squeeze started when a country issued an RFP for conversion services and nobody bid, after years at an unprofitable $4/kg.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Failed RFPs are the canary for supply-side squeezes in the fuel cycle.
insights.quote: one of the countries went out and put out for conversion services and nobody bid

insights.claim: The front-end nuclear fuel cycle is about 25% of reactor generating costs and uranium is only mid-single to low-double digits percent, versus 80-90% fuel share for coal and natural gas, so fuel buyers are price-insensitive.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Low price elasticity of demand means prices can spike sharply before demand responds.

insights.claim: In 2017 fuel buyers cited about 1.4 billion pounds of inventory, but Alkin's work concluded only about 400-500 million pounds was mobile, with the rest in depleted tails, sovereign stockpiles or otherwise not reaching the market.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Headline inventory figures overstate available supply; mobile inventory is far smaller.

insights.claim: After Alkin began arguing in 2017 that uneconomic mines must close, about 25% of world supply came offline over the following 18 months.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Validates the thesis that sub-economic prices remove supply.

insights.claim: Fuel buyers, mostly nuclear engineers, are not compensated for calling price bottoms and are not commercially incentivized, so they buy at peaks and under-contract when prices are low.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Buyer behavior is pro-cyclical, amplifying price spikes once contracting resumes.

insights.claim: At the latest NEI conference Alkin could not find a single uranium bear to debate; fuel buyers now accept higher prices but rely on new supply such as NexGen and Denison coming online in 2028-2030, which he says does not solve the structural deficit.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Consensus buyer hope rests on new mines; any delay at these projects tightens the market further.

insights.claim: Townsend expects buyers who were never paid to time the market will panic-contract when career risk of running out of fuel dominates; Alkin agrees they will be late, citing conversion up about 15x and enrichment about 7x as precedents.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host)
insights.so_what: A late-cycle contracting panic is a plausible upside scenario for uranium.

themes.theme: Upside wildcards: price history, SMRs, hyperscalers, new builds

insights.claim: In the last cycle uranium rose from $7/lb in 2000 to $137 spot in 2007 (about $200 in today's dollars) with a contract high near $95, despite a supply surplus over the following five years; today the same exercise shows massive deficits.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: If prices hit about $200 real in surplus, a deficit market implies substantially higher potential.

insights.claim: Townsend's 'lightwater leapfrog' thesis: factory-built Generation 4 reactors (Aalo is building a factory in Georgetown, Texas to mass-produce 100 reactors a year, promised for 2029) could reach behind-the-meter users before the next AP1000 is built.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host)
insights.so_what: Advanced reactors could pull uranium demand forward well ahead of 2040s expectations.

insights.claim: If advanced reactor demand materializes early, Alkin says prices would have to rise far beyond current expectations to unlock depleted tails, stockpiles and uneconomic shallow low-grade mines, such as some in Africa.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Additional demand would push the incentive price much higher.

insights.claim: Townsend predicts hyperscalers investing in advanced reactors will realize the fuel, not the reactor, is the constraint, and may seek full offtake agreements for mines such as NexGen's.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host)
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler offtake deals would be a major catalyst for developers.

insights.claim: Alkin flags executive orders and talk of 10 to 20 new reactors to be started by 2030; a utility announcing a new build could send uranium 'off to the races' and scare bears.
insights.speaker: Mike Alkin
insights.so_what: Watch for new-build announcements as an offset to AI-driven selling.
insights.quote: there's talks of up to 10 to 20 reactors that want to be started by 2030

themes.theme: Market desk: SPUT discount trade and macro

insights.claim: Physical uranium trusts trade at a large discount, with Townsend citing about 18% below NAV for SPUT, offering uranium below market price.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host)
insights.so_what: Buying physical via discounted trust provides uranium exposure plus discount-narrowing upside.

insights.claim: Patrick Ceresna's trade on Sprott Physical Uranium Trust (U.UN in Canada, reference C$26.60, NAV about C$31.50) is a Jan 15, 2027 C$25/C$28 bull call spread for a C$1.60 debit, max profit C$1.40 if the discount narrows to about 10% (about C$28.35).
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna (market desk)
insights.so_what: Defined-risk way to play discount narrowing without needing uranium to rally.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 corrected about 7% peak to trough while the NASDAQ fell about 16% and the semiconductor ETF SMH fell about 30%, with breadth still strong at about 71% of stocks above their 50-day moving averages, indicating the selloff is concentrated in AI.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna (market desk)
insights.so_what: AI-centered selloff with healthy breadth suggests rotation rather than broad bear market so far.

insights.claim: October CPI came in hot at 0.4% month over month (0.3% core), and Waller suggested a December tightening, possibly 50 basis points, causing bonds to break down and the dollar to break out against major currencies.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna (market desk)
insights.so_what: Hawkish Fed and stronger dollar are headwinds for risk assets including commodity equities.

insights.claim: WTI oil dropped from about $105 to the mid-$80s post-election, removing about $20 of risk premium despite depleted global inventories; gold remains in a primary downtrend with downside risk toward $3,600.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna (market desk)
insights.so_what: Oil re-escalation risk could re-ignite inflation; respect gold's downtrend until it reverses.
